families.s: HSE vehicle exhaust and diesel-emission control guidance for workshops
families.t: carbon monoxide, diesel carcinogens, static running, tailpipe extraction, ventilation discharge, leaks, cold engines, catalytic converters and exposure duration
f: Vehicle exhaust fumes can irritate the eyes and respiratory tract.
Carbon-fuelled engines emit carbon monoxide, which is poisonous.
Long-term repeated exposure to diesel exhaust can increase lung-cancer risk.
Static-running vehicles should use tailpipe exhaust extraction, particularly near inspection pits.
Extracted fumes should discharge outdoors where they cannot re-enter or affect others.
Flexible hoses and couplings should be maintained to prevent leaks.
Open workshop doors should not be relied upon as the ventilation control.
Catalytic converters do not make indoor engine running safe, especially when engines and catalysts are cold.
families.g: Exhaust risk depends on engine and fuel, operating temperature and duration, indoor volume and ventilation, tailpipe extraction and discharge, equipment condition, occupancy and exposure frequency.

families.s: HSE roadside vehicle repair and recovery traffic-risk guidance
families.t: road traffic, safe systems, vehicle occupants, public protection, winches, cranes, attachments, visibility, task minimisation and recovery location
f: Roadside repair and recovery workers face significant risk from passing road users.
Safe systems should protect workers and the occupants of vehicles being repaired or recovered.
Work activities must also safeguard other people who may be affected.
Recovery vehicles, winches, cranes and attachments may require controls beyond ordinary roadworthiness testing.
The site and traffic conditions should be assessed before people leave the recovery vehicle or begin work.
Warning, positioning, visibility and exclusion arrangements should suit the road environment.
Air-suspension work at the roadside should be limited and should never rely on ride-height pressure for support.
Where a repair cannot be completed safely, the vehicle should be recovered to an adequately equipped facility.
families.g: Roadside-recovery risk depends on road and traffic conditions, visibility and weather, vehicle position, task duration, recovery equipment, exclusion and communication, vehicle condition and competence.

families.s: HSE used-engine-oil skin exposure and hygiene guidance
families.t: dermatitis, skin cancer, contact avoidance, nitrile gloves, oily rags, protective clothing, washing, skin care and health monitoring
f: Frequent or prolonged contact with used engine oil can cause dermatitis and other skin disorders.
Long-term skin contact may also increase skin-cancer risk.
Unnecessary contact with used oil should be avoided through safe work methods.
Suitable protective clothing and nitrile gloves can reduce contamination.
Oily rags should not be kept in pockets because oil can soak through clothing onto skin.
Contaminated clothing should be cleaned or replaced regularly.
High standards of handwashing and personal hygiene are required.
Skin-care products can assist cleaning and replenishment, but barrier creams are not a substitute for effective protection.
families.g: Used-oil risk depends on oil contamination and additives, frequency and duration of contact, splash and wiping tasks, gloves and clothing, hygiene, skin condition and supervision.

families.s: HSE motor-repair petrol, fuel-draining and fire-explosion guidance
families.t: petrol vapour, tank draining, fuel retrievers, pits, waste oil, hot work, flammable thinners, ignition control and emergency response
f: Motor-repair fires and explosions can cause fatal injury and major property damage.
Many incidents involve mishandling petrol while draining tanks or fuel lines.
A proprietary fuel retriever should be used for draining petrol from vehicles.
Recovered petrol should not be mixed into waste-oil storage.
Petrol tanks should not be drained near or over an inspection pit.
Hot work can ignite residues or vapour in fuel tanks, lines and nearby containers.
Waste thinners or petrol must not be used to start or assist rubbish fires.
Flammable-liquid handling, ventilation, ignition control and emergency arrangements should be planned together.
families.g: Motor-repair fire risk depends on fuel and vapour inventory, draining and transfer method, pits and ventilation, hot work and ignition, storage and waste, housekeeping and emergency control.

families.s: HSE motor-vehicle hot-work, wheel and flame-cutting safety guidance
families.t: welding, flame cutting, wheels and tyres, tanks and containers, coatings, fume extraction, fire watch, isolation and confined locations
f: Hot work on wheels can create explosion risk if heat reaches an inflated tyre or contaminated assembly.
Tyres should be removed or fully deflated and the wheel made safe before heat is applied.
Welding and flame cutting are used for component repair and releasing seized parts.
Paint, underseal and other coatings can create hazardous fume during hot work.
Local exhaust ventilation should be used wherever practicable.
Extraction is essential in confined locations and for higher-hazard welding processes.
Fuel tanks, drums and containers that contain or have contained flammable liquid require specialist safe preparation before hot work.
Fire prevention, removal of combustibles, isolation and post-work checks should be included in the permit or safe system.
families.g: Motor hot-work risk depends on wheel and tyre condition, fuel or residue, coating and metal, heat and sparks, ventilation and extraction, confined space, isolation, fire precautions and competence.
